(back) to the ROOM'); the remaining 31 have exactly one mention, 0 had no literal regex hit. Across all 68 items with at least one hit, the LAST mention's room matches the gold target in EVERY case (68/68, 0 disagreements) -- when a person moves more than once, only their most recent move is ever the right answer. Every demonstration below is therefore told explicitly to take the LAST reported location, never the first.

chunks.summary: Chapters X–XXI follow Cameron and companions through the Canadian West during growing Indigenous unrest and the 1885 Rebellion. Raven rescues Moira from a runaway wagon; neighbors build the Camerons a house; Mandy nurses a sick Piegan boy; Cameron investigates conspirators in Sun Dance Canyon, arrests Eagle Feather, and later captures Sioux leader Copperhead. Raven, an outlaw but secretly loyal, saves stolen cattle and dies protecting Cameron, Moira, and the Queen. Cameron escapes captivity with Jerry and patrols the Ghost River region while Crowfoot’s loyalty helps prevent wider war. After rebellion ends, Cameron and Moira’s family prosper, and Dr. Martin finally declares his love for Moira. The appended articles discuss fireproof initiation rites, American building stones, farming, lime kilns, apple-jelly manufacture, grape bags, solar heat, surveying meridians, pheasants, trees, and American woods. A Shire-horse manual emphasizes sound mares, superior sires, and responsible breeding.

The Shire text advocates early breeding, outdoor rearing, wholesome feeding, careful hoof care, humane handling, training young horses for farm work, and honest breeding for soundness and utility. It traces Shire origins, Flemish influence, shows, prices, exports, prominent studs, and wartime prospects.

Gabriel Carew leaves Doctor Louis’s house in Nerac, visits the Three Black Crows, follows two suspected thieves into the woods, and later discovers one dead outside the doctor’s house. The wounded survivor is captured, confesses under hypnosis, and is executed. Carew marries Lauretta, while Eric is murdered and Emilius is accused.

In Peru, Sam, Jimmie, and Carl fly the *Ann* from Quito to a mountain valley, investigate a supposedly haunted temple, find beds and food inside, and discover hidden passages apparently used to stage ghostly warnings connected with Redfern.

Carl and Jimmie enter a dark temple apartment and are trapped behind a newly installed iron gate. They discover that the supposed supernatural phenomena are caused by hidden passages, staged lights, and captive jaguars. Four jaguars attack; the boys shoot some, but Carl is wounded and Jimmie runs out of ammunition. Outside, Sam Weller finds the _Ann_ moved into a thicket, overpowers a conspirator, and enters the temple with him. Indians kill Felix, while Sam learns the boys were thrown to the animals. He reaches the barred chamber, kills the final jaguar, rescues the boys, and obtains the key from Pedro. The boys later crawl through a secret passage from the animal den to the forest, reach the _Ann_, retrieve food and ammunition, and return through the tunnel to save Sam from attacking Indians. The group eventually captures Redfern at a mountain fortress and exposes the “Mystery of the Andes” as an electrical deception.

The text describes the Transvaal’s gold boom, Johannesburg’s rapid growth, Uitlander grievances, Cecil Rhodes’s ambitions, and the failed Jameson Raid, which deepened Boer-British hostility. It portrays rural Boers as pastoral, religious, isolated, hospitable, skilled marksmen, and led diplomatically by President Kruger. Kruger’s interview in his Pretoria cottage presents the Boer case for independence, while Rhodes’s career centers on mining monopolies, imperial expansion, and Groote Schuur. The Boer government, Volksraads, military mobilization, fortifications, and preparations for war are detailed, alongside American commercial and engineering influence. Johannesburg is depicted as cosmopolitan, wealthy, expensive, speculative, dusty, and socially divided. The latter medical material discusses hereditary syphilis and numerous mouth and tongue diseases, including stomatitis, thrush, gangrene, mercury poisoning, glossitis, ulcers, and macroglossia, emphasizing diagnosis and historical treatments.

The text reviews infant dentition, describing eruption timing, normal variations, salivation, local gum inflammation, aphthae, systemic reflex symptoms, convulsions, and treatment. It then discusses tonsillitis and pharyngitis—their varieties, causes, symptoms, complications, diagnosis, prognosis, and historical treatments. Esophageal diseases include acute and chronic inflammation, ulcers, spasmodic and organic strictures, cancer, paralysis, and dilation. Gastric sections examine functional dyspepsia, gastralgia, acute and chronic gastritis, and simple gastric ulcer, emphasizing diet, hygiene, nervous influences, hemorrhage, perforation, and supportive or medicinal care. The text also states: “Sandra moved to the kitchen.”

The text reviews gastric ulcer, gastric cancer, hemorrhage, and gastric dilatation. Gastric ulcer may remain latent, follow a chronic course, heal with deforming scars, or cause fatal perforation, hemorrhage, abscesses, fistulas, peritonitis, and pyloric stenosis. Its causes remain uncertain, with circulatory injury and digestion by gastric juice prominent theories. Diagnosis relies on characteristic epigastric pain, vomiting, and hematemesis; treatment emphasizes rest, bland liquid nutrition, rectal feeding when necessary, symptom control, and cautious surgery for perforation or obstruction. Gastric cancer usually affects older adults, especially the pyloric region, producing anorexia, pain, vomiting, coffee-ground emesis, tumor, progressive wasting, anemia, cachexia, and metastases. It is generally fatal, though rare surgical resection may prolong life. Gastric dilatation results from pyloric obstruction, excessive or fermenting contents, or muscular weakness, causing delayed vomiting, retained food, fermentation, splashing sounds, and emaciation; treatment centers on dietary restriction and stomach-tube irrigation.

The text surveys gastric anomalies and rupture, rejecting “gastromalacia” as a disease occurring during life. It then explains intestinal digestion, emphasizing bile, pancreatic and intestinal juices, absorption, and causes of intestinal indigestion such as diet, anemia, stress, sedentary habits, constipation, and disease of the liver or pancreas. Symptoms include delayed abdominal pain, gas, altered stools, malnutrition, anemia, nervous disturbances, and wasting; treatment centers on rest, regulated meals, careful mastication, exercise, climate change, bathing, milk-based diets, and limited medicines. Constipation is defined as prolonged or difficult evacuation, caused by diet, inactivity, disease, habit, or obstruction, and may produce fecal impaction, dilation, ulcers, and systemic symptoms. Enteralgia, intestinal catarrh, chronic diarrhea, cholera morbus, and summer diarrhea in children are also described, with emphasis on hygiene, safe food and water, breastfeeding, cooling, rest, and supportive treatment. Recommended travel includes trips to Europe, seashores, mountains, and therapeutic springs in Virginia or Arkansas.

The text reviews infantile summer diarrhea and cholera infantum, emphasizing watery stools, vomiting, dehydration, fever, rapid wasting, intestinal inflammation, prognosis, hygiene, breast milk, carefully prepared substitutes, and historical treatments. It then discusses pseudo-membranous enteritis: chronic mucus-cast production, predominantly in nervous women, diagnosis, pathology, and treatment. Dysentery is described as inflammatory ulceration of the colon with tenesmus, mucus, blood, and pus; causes include infection, climate, sanitation, contaminated water, and diet, with treatment centered on rest, hydration, irrigation, ipecacuanha, and supportive care. Further sections cover typhlitis, intestinal ulcers, hemorrhage, and obstruction, including intussusception, strictures, volvulus, and fecal impaction. The narrative states that **John travelled to the hallway**, **Daniel moved to the hallway**, and **Daniel moved to the kitchen**.

The text surveys Civil War campaigns from Shiloh through 1863. Confederate forces surprised Grant at Pittsburg Landing, but Buell and Lew Wallace arrived, enabling Union victory; Johnston was killed. McClellan advanced up Virginia’s Peninsula toward Richmond, fought at Seven Pines and Fair Oaks, then Lee’s Seven Days’ Battles forced him to Harrison’s Landing. Jackson’s Valley Campaign diverted Union forces, while Pope lost at Second Bull Run. Lee invaded Maryland but was checked at Antietam, prompting Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation. Union defeat followed at Fredericksburg and Chancellorsville, where Jackson was mortally wounded. Grant captured Vicksburg and Port Hudson, securing the Mississippi. Gettysburg halted Lee’s invasion of Pennsylvania. Subsequent fighting included Chickamauga and the struggle for Chattanooga.

The text surveys major Civil War campaigns: Chickamauga and Chattanooga, where Thomas held the “Rock” and Grant defeated Bragg; Grant and Lee’s Wilderness, Spotsylvania, Cold Harbor, and Petersburg campaigns; Sherman’s advance from Chattanooga to Atlanta, his March to the Sea, and campaign through the Carolinas; Sheridan’s Shenandoah victories; and the final collapse of the Confederacy. It recounts decisive battles, immense casualties, logistical innovation, devastation, and leadership by Thomas, Grant, Lee, Sherman, Sheridan, and others. Lee evacuated Richmond and Petersburg, retreated through Virginia, and surrendered to Grant at Appomattox on April 9, 1865. The text also includes dramatic scenes from a Belgian play about flooding dams to resist invading German forces, followed by a railroad-accident discussion emphasizing telegraphic safety, signaling failures, and collisions.

The text recounts numerous 19th-century railroad disasters, emphasizing derailments, bridge and drawbridge failures, collisions, inadequate brakes, signaling, discipline, and the need for automatic block and interlocking systems. It compares American, British, French, and Massachusetts safety statistics, arguing that rail travel was generally safer than stagecoach travel despite spectacular accidents. It then discusses Anglican teaching on the Prayer Book, Sacraments, Baptism, Confirmation, Marriage, and Holy Orders. In a fantasy episode, Jimmieboy and the sprite visit Fortyforefoot Valley; the major flees, is captured, and is held in an ice-box. Jimmieboy is locked in the castle pantry, frees the major, and later returns to the nursery couch, where he falls asleep; the major remains in the magical valley.

The text combines three works. First, it explains Anglican apostolic succession, episcopal and priestly ordination, jurisdiction, sacramental confession, absolution, and unction. It then reproduces extensive Victorian jokes, riddles, advertisements, and transcriber’s notes. A biography of Scottish doctor Elsie Inglis follows: she studied and practiced medicine in Edinburgh, trained in London, Dublin’s Rotunda, Paris, Vienna, and America, founded Edinburgh’s Hospice, campaigned for women’s suffrage, and organized Scottish Women’s Hospitals. She traveled to France, Serbia, and Russia, treating soldiers and civilians, especially during Serbia’s typhus epidemic. The text also describes Paris’s Latin Quarter, including the Luxembourg Gardens, studios, cafés, and Pochard’s decline.

The text chiefly recounts Dr. Elsie Inglis’s humanitarian career. After founding the Scottish Women’s Hospitals, she travelled to Serbia in 1915, treating typhus and wounded soldiers at Kragujevatz, Valjevo, Mladenovatz, Lazarevatz, and Krushieevatz. During the Austro-German invasion she remained with Serbian patients, endured captivity, and eventually travelled through Vienna and Bludenz to Zürich. In 1916–17 she led a women’s unit via Archangel and Moscow to Odessa, then served at Medgidia, Braila, Galatz, and Reni during the Romanian retreat and Russian Revolution. She evacuated with Serbian forces, travelling from Hadji Abdul through Russia to Archangel and Newcastle. Seriously ill, Inglis died soon after reaching Newcastle and was buried in Edinburgh, honoured by Scotland and Serbia. The text also contains unrelated excerpts about African adventures and Parisian student life.

The text combines three works. The first portrays Paris’s Latin Quarter: artists, models, cafés, cabarets, poverty, pleasure, the Luxembourg Gardens, and Bohemian life, ending with the narrator leaving his studio in a cab for the Gare St. Lazare. The second explains Anglican doctrine through the Prayer Book, emphasizing permanence and progress, the Sacraments, Baptism, Eucharist, Confirmation, Matrimony, Holy Orders, Penance, and Unction. The third presents Dutch colonial instructions for Jaffnapatam in 1697, covering taxation, trade, coinage, vessels, fortifications, food stores, military organization, labor, slavery, elephants, pearl fisheries, roads, water tanks, and governance. It concludes with Governor Gerrit de Heere’s comments, endorsing tighter administration, financial oversight, free-trade adjustments, grain supplies, and control over local populations and resources.

The first section reproduces Gerrit de Heere’s 1697 instructions for governing Dutch Jaffnapatam: regulate courts, debts, trade, currency, religion, fortifications, supplies, slavery, roads, elephants, horses, and land records, with strict oversight by the Dessave.

The later biography portrays Thomas Paine as a deist and humanitarian imprisoned during the French Terror. Arrested at the Passage des Petits Pères, he was taken to Rue Jacob and the Great Britain Hotel, then to the Luxembourg prison. After Monroe secured his release, Paine stayed at the Monroes’ house, later recovered with friends, helped found Theophilanthropy, defended reason and religious liberty, criticized Washington’s silence, and continued advocating republicanism, social justice, and peace.

Thomas Paine’s later life saw him move from revolutionary prominence to poverty, religious controversy, and social ostracism. After living with the Bonnevilles in Paris, he travelled to Belgium, returned to Paris, and sailed from Havre to Baltimore in 1802, then visited Washington, Bordentown, New York, Stonington, and his farm at New Rochelle. He defended republicanism, deism, abolition, Louisiana’s purchase, and neutral commerce, while pursuing bridge and steam inventions. In America he faced mobs, denied voting rights, financial hardship, illness, and slander from Cheetham and Carver. He died peacefully in Greenwich, New York, in 1809, maintaining his beliefs; his remains were later exhumed by Cobbett. The appended fiction follows Frank Blaisdell, whose lost fortune restores him to useful work, while the Blaisdell family relocates to Plainville. Miss Maggie and Mr. Smith finally confess love, though Smith’s identity as Stanley Fulton remains startlingly undisclosed.

Coningsby discovers his mother’s miniature in a banker’s box and meets Edith Millbank in Paris. Misreading Sidonia’s friendship with Edith, he leaves, but later learns the truth. He and Edith fall in love at Hellingsley; Millbank forbids their marriage because of his feud with Lord Monmouth. Coningsby rejects his grandfather’s demand to contest Darlford, is disinherited, and enters the Temple to study law. After Millbank nominates him, Coningsby wins Darlford and marries Edith at Millbank; Flora later leaves him her fortune. Meanwhile, Lord Monmouth separates from Lucretia and dies, leaving his estate to Flora. A separate narrative follows pirate Captain Flint, who operates from a crystal cave with Lightfoot and Black Bill. Haunted voices and apparitions frighten the crew, while Flint plans further piracy and disguises attacks as the work of another pirate.

Captain Flint’s pirate crimes are exposed when Henry Billings recognizes him and helps capture him at sea. Flint escapes prison, returns to his cave, kills Jones Bradley, and is later torn apart by a bear. Fire Cloud secretly rescues Hellena, Lightfoot, and Black Bill through a hidden passage from the cavern to an Indian village. Billings is mistakenly captured as Flint, delaying his reunion with Hellena, but they eventually return safely to New York. The cave’s “supernatural” noises are explained as echoes produced by Black Bill and Fire Cloud.

The remainder consists of John Evelyn’s diary: observations of London society, religious and political conflict, royal deaths and successions, the Popish Plot, the Monmouth rebellion, persecution of Protestants, James II’s Catholic policies, the imprisonment and acquittal of the bishops, and William of Orange’s invasion and accession.

The text combines excerpts from several historical works: John Evelyn’s diary (1689–1705), describing political upheaval, religious disputes, wars, weather, scientific and cultural life, family deaths, and the founding of Greenwich Hospital; memoirs of Minnesota’s territorial printers, Civil War service, and St. Paul society; accounts of the battles of Mill Springs and Pittsburg Landing; a young woman’s diaries recording family, weddings, travel, religious life, and her grandmother’s death; and essays comparing Maya, Egyptian, African, Asian, and American cultures, especially writing, mythology, customs, and music. It also includes advertisements, market reports, bibliographical notices, and editorial corrections. Notable movements include Evelyn’s visits to London, Lambeth, Wotton, Deptford, Kensington, Eton, and Greenwich; the diarist’s travels through England, Scotland, Paris, and America; and soldiers’ movements through Kentucky, Tennessee, Mississippi, and the Dakotas.

The first section surveys medieval and post-medieval musical instruments: lyres, psalteries, harps, rottas, fiddles, organs, wind instruments, bells, carillons, lutes, viols, and related orchestras, emphasizing their evolution, regional variation, and historical evidence.

The novel follows Jessica Lawton’s millinery shop and charitable Girls’ Resting House, Kate Minster’s support, and Horace Boyce’s morally corrupt ambitions. Tenney and Wendover manipulate the Minster fortune through fraudulent industrial schemes, while Reuben Tracy uncovers the conspiracy and helps Kate and Ethel. After the mills close and workers threaten violence, Jessica learns of a mob and seeks Reuben. She finds Horace in a lawyer’s office, then travels with Gedney in a sleigh to Reuben’s mother’s farmhouse, where Reuben is visiting his sick mother.

Jessica Lawton travels to Reuben Tracy’s mother’s farm, rescues him for the threatened Minster estate, steals Gedney’s affidavits, and leaves the mob at the Minster house. Reuben pacifies the crowd, then learns Jessica has collapsed at General Boyce’s house; dying, she reconciles Horace and Reuben and reveals their child.

Other tales follow Cissy Trixit fleeing her seized Canada City home to find her fugitive father, and Masterton pursuing her through the Sierras. At a fonda, Cota’s horse attacks men, inspiring a ghost legend. On Eureka Mountain, Eugenia falls onto Bray, whose companions discover gold; “Jack” and “Jill” reunite in San Francisco. Miss Trotter’s hotel career and Chris Calton’s failed engagement lead to their love. Lester Kane takes Jennie from Cleveland to New York and Chicago, concealing her daughter Vesta.

Jennie’s concealed daughter, Vesta, is discovered, forcing her to confess her past to Lester. He brings Vesta into their Chicago apartment, later moves the household to a Hyde Park home, and accepts Jennie’s father Gerhardt there. Social condemnation, family pressure, and his father’s will eventually compel Lester to separate from Jennie so he can reclaim his fortune. Jennie moves with Vesta to a cottage in Sandwood; after Vesta dies of typhoid, Jennie returns to Chicago. Lester, having married Letty Gerald and regained wealth, falls ill in the Auditorium Hotel and summons Jennie, confessing that she was the only woman he truly loved. He dies shortly afterward, while Jennie watches his funeral procession and train depart for Cincinnati. The appended theological chapters explain Baptism, Eucharist, and Confirmation as sacramental unions of matter and spirit, emphasizing their essentials, saving grace, regeneration, adoption, election, communion, and the laying on of hands.

The text combines several works. A religious manual explains Holy Matrimony, Holy Order, Penance, and Unction, emphasizing consent, Apostolic Succession, clerical roles, confession, absolution, and healing. Historical chapters recount Lord Durham’s Canadian mission, the rebellions of 1837–38, battles at Lacolle and Odelltown, executions, and later reconciliation. Fiction follows Winton’s “S. W. F. Club,” whose members explore the village, visit the manor, picnic at The Maples and an old fort, and prepare to leave for school. Another story describes Minnie’s mischievous pet monkey Jacko. A Cornish travel narrative records visits to the Lizard, Lizard Lights, Marazion, St. Michael’s Mount, Land’s End, Whitesand Bay, Tintagel, and Boscastle. Finally, on the Big Horn Ranch, Allan and Mandy go fishing, rescue an injured Piegan boy, and meet his returning companions.

Mandy and Allan Cameron rescue a Piegan boy, then learn that the aristocratic Chief Onawata—“Copperhead”—is plotting an uprising. Cameron and Inspector Dickson fail to arrest him at the Piegan camp; Copperhead burns the ranch, but Mandy survives. Cameron later pursues him through Calgary, the Sun Dance Canyon, and Indigenous reserves while Mandy, Moira, Dr. Martin, Smith, and allies support the rebuilding of the ranch. Moira and Martin fall in love; outlaw Raven saves her from a runaway wagon and later dies helping Cameron stop a cattle stampede. During the wider 1885 rebellion, Cameron captures Copperhead after escaping captivity with Jerry. The Police prevent a western Indigenous uprising, while the appended diary shifts abruptly to 1865 American Civil War news, Lincoln’s assassination, Booth’s death, Davis’s capture, church life, and local social observations.
